document_metadata.document_title: Indiana Storm Water Quality Manual (city MS4 / IDEM reference)

design_criteria.water_quality_volume_method: Treat at least one-half inch of storm water runoff (water quality volume or storage) from impervious surfaces, targeting ≥80% TSS removal on an annual average basis; post-development peak discharge rates and volumes should not exceed predevelopment levels.

evidence.excerpt: South Bend MS4 references Indiana Storm Water Quality Manual
Treat at least one-half inch of storm water runoff
Water Quality Volume (WQV). The volume of runoff generated by one inch of rainfall on a site.
The pond should contain a low-flow drain with an adjustable gate valve allowing for gradual discharge. Recommended drawdown is 24 hours.
evidence.page_or_section: Chapter 8, Wet Detention Ponds, Table 3, page 639

evidence.excerpt: Bottom of the basin > 3 feet above the seasonal high water table depth
The bottom of the bioretention area should be three feet or more above the seasonal high water table
Aeration and drainage for planting bed is provided by a 12 to 20-inch deep sand and/or gravel bed.
Any system wider than 20 feet should be at least twice as long to evenly distribute the flow.

extraction_quality.review_notes: Municipality coverage via Indiana Storm Water Quality Manual (Evansville pattern).

design_parameters.enrich_notes: Atlas (South Bend) cites treating at least 0.5 inch of runoff from impervious surfaces; manual glossary defines WQV as runoff from one inch of rainfall. Small-storm treatment sizing for pervious pavement, infiltration trench, and infiltration basin references typically 0.5–1.5 inches (not a single mandated depth). SHWT separation of 3 feet appears for bioretention, infiltration basin, infiltration trench, porous pavement reservoirs, wet ponds, and constructed wetlands. Bioretention ponding recommended 6–9 inches (range only). Wet extended detention variant releases over 12–48 hours (range only).
